title: It can rise
hook: Seneca on the burned city of Lyon: cities, and people, can rise again (Letters 91)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Yad Vashem, a place and a name that shall not be cut off. Your line was remember. After the days of mourning, a letter about rebuilding.

Word arrives from far away, and there is nothing anyone can do but read it. A city in Gaul, the colony the Romans called Lugdunum, the place we call Lyon, has burned. A man named Liberalis, who has ties to the city, is crushed. His friend Seneca, the Stoic writer, hears about it, and sits down to write a letter to another friend, Lucilius. It begins with Liberalis's grief, and it doesn't wave it away.
screen: `A CITY IN GAUL HAS BURNED.` → `LIBERALIS IS CRUSHED.` → `SENECA PICKS UP A PEN.`

segments.voice: First, one night. Seneca is struck by how fast it happened. In his telling, a single night stood between a great city and no city at all. Everything a city builds slowly, a fire can take quickly. He doesn't pretend otherwise. Second, expect it. Seneca's advice is an old Stoic one: let the mind rehearse what could happen, so that loss, when it comes, doesn't come as a total stranger. Nothing, he says, should be unexpected by us. That can sound cold. In the letter it reads more like a friend saying: we live in a world where things fall, and you are allowed to know that ahead of time. Third, it can rise. Here the letter turns. Seneca reminds Lucilius that cities have been leveled before, by fire and by earthquake, and have been raised again, and that the ruin can make room for something better. He hopes the same for Lyon. Not the same city. A city, rising. Fourth, people too. The letter moves on from the city to human lives, to bodies and their endings. Some readers carry his turn over to a person: what falls in a life can sometimes be rebuilt, slowly, stone by stone. This is not a promise that every loss gets fixed. Yesterday's names belong to people who can never be given their lives back, and grief like that doesn't need a happy ending. Seneca's point is narrower. Ruin is real, and so is rebuilding. Both belong to the world. Today, after days of mourning, the second half gets its turn.
screen: `ONE NIGHT BETWEEN A CITY AND NONE.` · `LET NOTHING COME AS A STRANGER.` · `CITIES HAVE RISEN AGAIN.` · `PEOPLE, TOO, STONE BY STONE.` · then, large: `IT CAN RISE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing in your life that has fallen down: a habit you dropped, a shelf that collapsed, a friendship gone quiet, a garden left to weeds. Look at it honestly, as Seneca looks at Lyon, then picture the first stone going back: one text, one drawer sorted, one seed in the ground. Just the first stone, and breathe with that picture.
Seneca, writing to Lucilius about a burned city, Lyon, and the hope that what falls can be built again. Today's word.
Your line: a city, rising. Ruin is real, and so is the first stone. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Stoics turn to Seneca's letters in hard seasons, using his practice of rehearsing possible losses in advance, and his reminder that what falls can be rebuilt.

chat.says: Our town flooded last spring. Is it silly to hope it comes back?
options: Seneca wrote that cities leveled by fire have risen again. Ruin's real; so is rebuilding.
It's silly. Once a place is ruined, it's gone for good, and that's that.
Hoping means it will surely come back exactly as it was, stone for stone.
chat.meaning: Seneca reminds Lucilius that cities leveled by fire and earthquake have been raised again. Ruin is real, and so is rebuilding.
